findings.summary: 2D to 3D conversion transforms flat film into stereoscopic imagery by generating separate views for each eye. The process relies on creating depth maps—grayscale images indicating per-pixel depth—to shift original pixels laterally. High-quality methods allocate a "depth budget," segment surfaces, assign depth values, synthesize stereo pairs via 2D-plus-depth rendering, and fill uncovered areas. Lower-quality automatic conversion serves cheap 3DTV and VOD. Computer-animated films with accessible source data can be re-rendered using a second virtual camera, achieving quality comparable to native stereo. The technique is widely used for non-CGI blockbusters, though stereo post-production is complex and costly compared to 2D workflows.

mechanisms.title: Depth-map-based stereo generation
mechanisms.explanation: A depth map, a grayscale image matching the original 2D frame, encodes per-pixel depth. Pixels are shifted left or right based on this map and a target parallax setting, synthesizing left and right eye views. This 2D-plus-depth approach inherently cannot represent semi-transparent surfaces or occluded geometry, often resulting in a 2.5D appearance.

mechanisms.title: Depth budget allocation and scene segmentation
mechanisms.explanation: Conversion workflows must define the range of permitted disparity, set the screen-plane convergence point, and isolate important surfaces via segmentation or rotoscoping. Each surface receives a depth map composed into a scene map, with micro-relief added to prevent a "cardboard" effect. Uncovered areas from differing view angles are filled via inpainting or artist work, as exact reconstruction is generally impossible.

unknowns: How automation techniques generate accurate depth maps for translucent or reflective objects
The specific algorithms used to fill uncovered areas without introducing visual artifacts
Whether depth micro-relief can be reliably added to organic subjects like hair or fur
The practical limits of depth budget allocation when stereo mismatches are large
